    A sequence begins 8, 13, 18, 23, …8,\ 13,\ 18,\ 23,\ \ldots8, 13, 18, 23, … and each term after the first adds the same amount. What is a11a_{11}a11​?

    Answer choices for question 1

    Solution

    Correct answer: B

    You chose A: Adds nd=11(5)nd = 11(5)nd=11(5) to a1a_1a1​, taking 111111 steps from the first term instead of the n−1=10n-1 = 10n−1=10 that separate the eleventh term from it.

    You chose C: Multiplies the 101010 steps by ddd but never adds the first term a1=8a_1 = 8a1​=8.

    You chose D: Takes only 999 steps (8+9(5)8 + 9(5)8+9(5)), stopping one position short at the tenth term.

    The common difference is d=13−8=5d = 13 - 8 = 5d=13−8=5, and reaching the eleventh term takes n−1=10n - 1 = 10n−1=10 steps from the first.

    a11=8+(11−1)(5)=8+50=58a_{11} = 8 + (11 - 1)(5) = 8 + 50 = 58a11​=8+(11−1)(5)=8+50=58

    A geometric sequence has a1=4a_1 = 4a1​=4 and a5=324a_5 = 324a5​=324. Which statement about its common ratio rrr is correct?

    Answer choices for question 7

    Solution

    Correct answer: D

    You chose A: Takes only the positive fourth root of 818181, missing that an even power hides the sign of rrr.

    You chose B: Reads rrr off as 818181 itself rather than taking the fourth root of r4=81r^{4} = 81r4=81.

    You chose C: Concludes the ratio is undetermined, when the two terms pin it down to exactly two values.

    Positions 111 and 555 are 444 steps apart, so 324=4r4324 = 4 r^{4}324=4r4 gives r4=81r^{4} = 81r4=81, an even power that keeps both signs.

    r4=81⟹r=±3r^{4} = 81 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad r = \pm 3r4=81⟹r=±3

    Both 4,12,36,108,3244, 12, 36, 108, 3244,12,36,108,324 and 4,−12,36,−108,3244, -12, 36, -108, 3244,−12,36,−108,324 fit, so rrr is 333 or −3-3−3.

    Exactly one of these infinite series has a finite sum. Which one?

    Answer choices for question 12

    Solution

    Correct answer: D

    You chose A: Sees a clear geometric pattern and assumes it totals, but r=2r = 2r=2 makes the terms grow, so no finite sum exists.

    You chose B: Treats a constant series as convergent, but adding 777 forever (r=1r = 1r=1) grows without bound.

    You chose C: Reads the running total as settling near 555, but with r=−1r = -1r=−1 it flips between 555 and 000 forever.

    An infinite geometric series settles exactly when ∣r∣<1|r| < 1∣r∣<1. The four ratios are 222, 111, −1-1−1, and 13\frac{1}{3}31​, and only the last satisfies the condition.

    ∣13∣<1⟹S=91−13=272\left|\tfrac{1}{3}\right| < 1 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad S = \frac{9}{1 - \frac{1}{3}} = \frac{27}{2}​31​​<1⟹S=1−31​9​=227​

    Two infinite sums are built the same way, by adding shrinking pieces: ∑k=1∞(k+1−k)\displaystyle\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}\left(\sqrt{k+1} - \sqrt{k}\right)k=1∑∞​(k+1​−k​) and ∑k=1∞(1k−1k+1)\displaystyle\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}\left(\dfrac{1}{k} - \dfrac{1}{k+1}\right)k=1∑∞​(k1​−k+11​). Which one has a finite value?

    Answer choices for question 16

    Solution

    Correct answer: B

    You chose A: Assumes the square-root sum settles, but its surviving tail n+1\sqrt{n+1}n+1​ grows without bound instead of shrinking.

    You chose C: Assumes telescoping alone guarantees a finite value; it does not unless the surviving tail shrinks to zero.

    You chose D: Overlooks that the second's tail 1n+1\frac{1}{n+1}n+11​ shrinks to zero, so it does settle, at 111.

    Both telescope, so what decides settling is whether the surviving tail shrinks to zero. The first collapses to n+1−1\sqrt{n+1} - 1n+1​−1, whose tail grows; the second collapses to 1−1n+11 - \frac{1}{n+1}1−n+11​, whose tail vanishes.

    n+1−1→∞,1−1n+1→1\sqrt{n+1} - 1 \to \infty, \qquad 1 - \frac{1}{n+1} \to 1n+1​−1→∞,1−n+11​→1

    The answer

    Part A

    a1=50a_1 = 50a1​=50, d=−6d = -6d=−6, and a12=−16a_{12} = -16a12​=−16.

    Part B

    n=26n = 26n=26: the 262626th term equals −100-100−100, because solving gives a positive whole number.

    Part C

    Going from a1a_1a1​ to a2a_2a2​ is a single step of ddd, and a1a_1a1​ itself sits at position 111 with zero steps taken, so reaching position nnn takes n−1n-1n−1 steps. Multiplying by nnn would count one step too many, overshooting every term after the first.

    Worked solution

    Part A

    The common difference is d=44−50=−6d = 44 - 50 = -6d=44−50=−6, and reaching the twelfth term takes n−1=11n - 1 = 11n−1=11 steps.

    a12=50+(12−1)(−6)=50−66=−16a_{12} = 50 + (12 - 1)(-6) = 50 - 66 = -16a12​=50+(12−1)(−6)=50−66=−16

    Part B

    Set the explicit formula equal to −100-100−100 and solve for nnn.

    50+(n−1)(−6)=−100⟹(n−1)(−6)=−150⟹n=2650 + (n - 1)(-6) = -100 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad (n - 1)(-6) = -150 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad n = 2650+(n−1)(−6)=−100⟹(n−1)(−6)=−150⟹n=26

    Since 262626 is a positive whole number, −100-100−100 is genuinely a term.

    Part C

    From a1=50a_1 = 50a1​=50 to a2=44a_2 = 44a2​=44 is one application of the step d=−6d = -6d=−6, not two, and a1a_1a1​ needed zero steps because it is where the counting starts.

    a2=a1+d,an=a1+(n−1)da_2 = a_1 + d, \qquad a_n = a_1 + (n - 1)da2​=a1​+d,an​=a1​+(n−1)d

    Following that count, position nnn is reached after exactly n−1n - 1n−1 steps, one fewer than the position number, which is why the formula multiplies ddd by n−1n - 1n−1.

    In one line

    For 50,44,38,32,…50, 44, 38, 32, \ldots50,44,38,32,…: a1=50a_1 = 50a1​=50, d=−6d = -6d=−6, and a12=−16a_{12} = -16a12​=−16; the value −100-100−100 is the 262626th term, since solving an=−100a_n = -100an​=−100 gives the positive whole number n=26n = 26n=26; and the formula uses n−1n-1n−1 steps because a1a_1a1​ takes zero steps and each later term adds exactly one.

    3. C
      Part C.

      Explain what feature of positions 222 and 444 made the ratio ambiguous here, and describe how the two given positions would have to differ for the ratio to be pinned down to a single value.

      Justify your claim State the claim, then give the reason it has to be true. 3 points

    The answer

    Part A

    r=12r = \dfrac{1}{2}r=21​ or r=−12r = -\dfrac{1}{2}r=−21​.

    Part B

    a1=24a_1 = 24a1​=24 when r=12r = \dfrac{1}{2}r=21​, and a1=−24a_1 = -24a1​=−24 when r=−12r = -\dfrac{1}{2}r=−21​.

    Part C

    Positions 222 and 444 are an even number of steps apart, so rrr satisfies an even power, r2=14r^2 = \frac{1}{4}r2=41​, which cannot distinguish a value from its negative. Had the two given positions been an odd number of steps apart, the equation for rrr would be an odd power, which fixes a single real value.

    Worked solution

    Part A

    Positions 222 and 444 are 222 steps apart, so a4=a2r2a_4 = a_2 r^{2}a4​=a2​r2. The power is even, so keep both signs of the root.

    3=12r2⟹r2=14⟹r=±123 = 12 r^{2} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad r^{2} = \frac{1}{4} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad r = \pm\frac{1}{2}3=12r2⟹r2=41​⟹r=±21​

    Part B

    The first term is one step before a2a_2a2​, so a1=a2ra_1 = \dfrac{a_2}{r}a1​=ra2​​. Divide 121212 by each carried-forward ratio.

    a1=121/2=24,a1=12−1/2=−24a_1 = \frac{12}{1/2} = 24, \qquad a_1 = \frac{12}{-1/2} = -24a1​=1/212​=24,a1​=−1/212​=−24

    Part C

    The gap is 4−2=24 - 2 = 24−2=2, an even number, so solving for rrr meant solving an even power, and an even power hides the sign:

    (12)2=(−12)2=14\left(\tfrac{1}{2}\right)^{2} = \left(-\tfrac{1}{2}\right)^{2} = \frac{1}{4}(21​)2=(−21​)2=41​

    An odd distance would give an odd power, which takes a unique real root, so the two terms would then determine rrr completely.

    In one line

    From a2=12a_2 = 12a2​=12 and a4=3a_4 = 3a4​=3, the ratio solves r2=14r^2 = \frac{1}{4}r2=41​, so r=12r = \frac{1}{2}r=21​ or r=−12r = -\frac{1}{2}r=−21​, giving a1=24a_1 = 24a1​=24 or a1=−24a_1 = -24a1​=−24. The ambiguity is because positions 222 and 444 are an even number of steps apart; an odd distance would fix rrr to a single value.

    130013001300; the range has 20−8+1=1320 - 8 + 1 = 1320−8+1=13 terms.

    Both endpoints are counted, so plain subtraction n−mn - mn−m counts only the gaps and leaves one endpoint out; adding it back gives n−m+1n - m + 1n−m+1 (here 20−8+1=1320 - 8 + 1 = 1320−8+1=13).     Part A

    Line 3. With a gap of 222, each negative piece cancels its partner two brackets later, so two pieces survive at each end: 12\frac{1}{2}21​ and 13\frac{1}{3}31​ at the front, 1n+2\frac{1}{n+2}n+21​ and 1n+3\frac{1}{n+3}n+31​ at the back, not one of each.

    In a gap-1 telescope the negative piece of a bracket is cancelled by the very next bracket, so all but the first and last cancel. In a gap-2 telescope the partner is two brackets away, so the first two positive pieces and the last two negative pieces never reach a partner and survive.

    With the delay of two, the first two positives and the last two negatives run off the end of the range with no partner, so two survive at each end.

Blair deposits 333 dollars on day 111 and each day after that deposits triple the previous day's deposit. These describe the daily deposits, not the running totals.

    Avery deposits 404040 dollars on day 666; Blair deposits 729729729 dollars on day 666.

      Part A.

      Part C.

    Part A

    ∣r∣=12<1\left|r\right| = \dfrac{1}{2} < 1∣r∣=21​<1, so the sum exists and equals 555.

    Part B

    0.72‾=7299=8110.\overline{72} = \dfrac{72}{99} = \dfrac{8}{11}0.72=9972​=118​.

    Part C

    The formula comes from the running total settling as terms are added, which happens only when the terms shrink, i.e. when ∣r∣<1|r| < 1∣r∣<1. For ∣r∣>1|r| > 1∣r∣>1 or r=−1r = -1r=−1 the terms do not shrink, so the fraction evaluates to a number that is a sum of nothing; at r=1r = 1r=1 it is undefined (1−r=01 - r = 01−r=0).

    The derivation depends on the later terms shrinking toward 000 as more are added, so that the running total approaches one value. That shrinking happens exactly when ∣r∣<1|r| < 1∣r∣<1.

    8. Two telescoping tails, and which one settles . 9 points. This question goes beyond core Algebra I. It is not required by the course. Question 8 of 10.

    9 pts Advanced. This question goes beyond core Algebra I. It is not required by the course.

    Two infinite telescoping sums are offered: ∑k=1∞(1k+3−1k+4)\displaystyle\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}\left(\frac{1}{k+3} - \frac{1}{k+4}\right)k=1∑∞​(k+31​−k+41​) and ∑k=1∞(k+1−k)\displaystyle\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}\left(\sqrt{k+1} - \sqrt{k}\right)k=1∑∞​(k+1​−k​).

    1. A
      Part A.

      Find the closed form of the first sum's first nnn terms, and state its value as nnn grows without bound.

      Write the expression An equation or an expression is enough here. Show how you built it. 3 points

    2. B
      Part B.

      Find the closed form of the second sum's first nnn terms, and state what happens as nnn grows without bound.

      Write the expression An equation or an expression is enough here. Show how you built it. 3 points

    3. C
      Part C.

      Both sums telescope to two survivors. Explain what actually decides whether an infinite telescoping sum has a finite value, and use it to say, for each of these two sums, whether it settles.

      Justify your claim State the claim, then give the reason it has to be true. 3 points

    The answer

    Part A

    14−1n+4\dfrac{1}{4} - \dfrac{1}{n+4}41​−n+41​, which approaches 14\dfrac{1}{4}41​ as nnn grows.

    Part B

    n+1−1\sqrt{n+1} - 1n+1​−1, which grows without bound as nnn grows.

    Part C

    What decides it is whether the surviving tail term shrinks to zero, not whether the sum telescopes. The first's tail 1n+4\frac{1}{n+4}n+41​ shrinks to zero, so it settles at 14\frac{1}{4}41​; the second's tail n+1\sqrt{n+1}n+1​ grows, so it never settles. Telescoping alone is not enough.

    Worked solution

    Part A

    With bk=1k+3b_k = \frac{1}{k+3}bk​=k+31​, the sum is a chain of bk−bk+1b_k - b_{k+1}bk​−bk+1​ that collapses to b1−bn+1b_1 - b_{n+1}b1​−bn+1​.

    ∑k=1n(1k+3−1k+4)=14−1n+4  ⟶  14\sum_{k=1}^{n}\left(\frac{1}{k+3} - \frac{1}{k+4}\right) = \frac{1}{4} - \frac{1}{n+4} \;\longrightarrow\; \frac{1}{4}∑k=1n​(k+31​−k+41​)=41​−n+41​⟶41​

    Part B

    This sum is already in mirror form bk+1−bkb_{k+1} - b_kbk+1​−bk​ with bk=kb_k = \sqrt{k}bk​=k​, so it collapses to the last value minus the first.

    ∑k=1n(k+1−k)=n+1−1  ⟶  ∞\sum_{k=1}^{n}\left(\sqrt{k+1} - \sqrt{k}\right) = \sqrt{n+1} - 1 \;\longrightarrow\; \infty∑k=1n​(k+1​−k​)=n+1​−1⟶∞

    Part C

    Both collapse to a fixed front piece and a moving tail. The value settles precisely when that tail shrinks to zero.

    14−1n+4→14(tail→0),n+1−1→∞(tail→∞)\frac{1}{4} - \frac{1}{n+4} \to \frac{1}{4} \quad (\text{tail} \to 0), \qquad \sqrt{n+1} - 1 \to \infty \quad (\text{tail} \to \infty)41​−n+41​→41​(tail→0),n+1​−1→∞(tail→∞)

    So the first is ruled in and the second ruled out; the deciding feature is the behavior of the surviving tail, not the fact of telescoping.

    In one line

    The first sum collapses to 14−1n+4\frac{1}{4} - \frac{1}{n+4}41​−n+41​, whose tail shrinks to zero, so it settles at 14\frac{1}{4}41​; the second collapses to n+1−1\sqrt{n+1} - 1n+1​−1, whose tail grows without bound, so it never settles. What decides an infinite telescoping sum is whether its surviving tail shrinks to zero, not that it telescopes.

      Part C.

      Explain what it means Words, not just symbols. Say what the number is telling you about the situation. 3 points

    The answer

    Part A

    The third bounce rises to 83\dfrac{8}{3}38​ feet.

    Part B

    454545 feet: the 999-foot drop, plus twice the infinite sum 6+4+83+⋯=186 + 4 + \dfrac{8}{3} + \cdots = 186+4+38​+⋯=18 for the up-and-down of every bounce.

    Part C

    Each bounce is 23\frac{2}{3}32​ of the last, so the rise heights form a geometric series with ∣r∣=23<1|r| = \frac{2}{3} < 1∣r∣=32​<1; the terms shrink fast enough that the running total settles instead of growing. Infinitely many terms add to a finite value precisely because ∣r∣<1|r| < 1∣r∣<1 makes them shrink toward zero.

    Worked solution

    Part A

    The first bounce rises to 9⋅23=69 \cdot \frac{2}{3} = 69⋅32​=6 feet, so the bounce heights are geometric with a1=6a_1 = 6a1​=6 and r=23r = \frac{2}{3}r=32​. The third bounce uses n−1=2n - 1 = 2n−1=2 factors.

    a3=6(23)2=6⋅49=83a_3 = 6 \left(\frac{2}{3}\right)^{2} = 6 \cdot \frac{4}{9} = \frac{8}{3}a3​=6(32​)2=6⋅94​=38​

    Part B

    After the initial 999-foot drop, every bounce rises and falls the same height, so the total is 999 plus twice the infinite geometric sum of the rise heights, with a1=6a_1 = 6a1​=6 and r=23r = \frac{2}{3}r=32​ (∣r∣<1|r| < 1∣r∣<1).

    9+2⋅61−23=9+2⋅18=459 + 2 \cdot \frac{6}{1 - \frac{2}{3}} = 9 + 2 \cdot 18 = 459+2⋅1−32​6​=9+2⋅18=45

    Part C

    The bounces never stop, but each is a fixed fraction of the last, so the rise heights shrink geometrically.

    ∣r∣=23<1⟹the total settles rather than growing without bound|r| = \frac{2}{3} < 1 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \text{the total settles rather than growing without bound}∣r∣=32​<1⟹the total settles rather than growing without bound

    Were the bounces to return to the same height each time (∣r∣=1|r| = 1∣r∣=1) or higher, the distance would grow without limit. The finite total is a direct consequence of ∣r∣<1|r| < 1∣r∣<1.

Infinitely many bounces add to a finite distance because ∣r∣=23<1|r| = \frac{2}{3} < 1∣r∣=32​<1 makes the rise heights shrink toward zero, so the running total settles.

    Two infinite series are given: a geometric series 13+19+127+⋯\dfrac{1}{3} + \dfrac{1}{9} + \dfrac{1}{27} + \cdots31​+91​+271​+⋯, and a telescoping series ∑k=1∞(1k−1k+1)\displaystyle\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}\left(\frac{1}{k} - \frac{1}{k+1}\right)k=1∑∞​(k1​−k+11​). This question sums each, then compares what makes each total exist.

      Part B.

      Part C.

      Justify your claim State the claim, then give the reason it has to be true. 5 points

    The answer

    Part A

    12\dfrac{1}{2}21​.

    Part B

    111: the finite sums 1−1n+11 - \dfrac{1}{n+1}1−n+11​ approach 111 as nnn grows.

    Part C

    The geometric series needs ∣r∣<1|r| < 1∣r∣<1; the telescope needs its surviving tail bn+1b_{n+1}bn+1​ to shrink to zero. Both share one requirement on what is left to add: that leftover must shrink to zero, so the total settles. The individual terms shrinking is not enough, as the square-root telescope shows.

    Worked solution

    Part A

    The ratio is r=13r = \frac{1}{3}r=31​, and ∣r∣<1|r| < 1∣r∣<1, so the infinite-sum formula applies.

    S=1/31−1/3=1/32/3=12S = \frac{1/3}{1 - 1/3} = \frac{1/3}{2/3} = \frac{1}{2}S=1−1/31/3​=2/31/3​=21​

    Part B

    With bk=1kb_k = \frac{1}{k}bk​=k1​, the sum collapses to b1−bn+1b_1 - b_{n+1}b1​−bn+1​, whose tail shrinks to zero.

    ∑k=1n(1k−1k+1)=1−1n+1  ⟶  1\sum_{k=1}^{n}\left(\frac{1}{k} - \frac{1}{k+1}\right) = 1 - \frac{1}{n+1} \;\longrightarrow\; 1∑k=1n​(k1​−k+11​)=1−n+11​⟶1

    Part C

    For the geometric series the stated condition is ∣r∣<1|r| < 1∣r∣<1; for the telescoping series it is that the surviving tail term shrinks to zero.

    geometric: ∣r∣<1  ⇒  a1rn→0,telescoping: bn+1→0\text{geometric: } |r| < 1 \;\Rightarrow\; a_1 r^{n} \to 0, \qquad \text{telescoping: } b_{n+1} \to 0geometric: ∣r∣<1⇒a1​rn→0,telescoping: bn+1​→0

    Both say the same thing about what is left to add: the remaining contribution must shrink toward zero. When it does, the running total settles on a finite value; when it does not, the total grows or refuses to settle.

    In one line

    The geometric series sums to 12\frac{1}{2}21​ (since ∣r∣=13<1|r| = \frac{1}{3} < 1∣r∣=31​<1) and the telescoping series sums to 111 (since 1−1n+1→11 - \frac{1}{n+1} \to 11−n+11​→1). Their conditions, ∣r∣<1|r| < 1∣r∣<1 and a vanishing surviving tail, are one requirement on what is left to add: that leftover must shrink to zero so the total settles.
